passage: Rain drummed on the fair tent, and the last bus was leaving soon. Papa Thomas's cloth bag had room for only one pot. He held up the shiny blue one he had bought at the stall. Noor, five, clutched her own lumpy clay pot. It was still damp at the edges, and one side sagged. "Mine!" she said. "Mine is the best one." "It might get squashed," Papa said. Noor pressed it to her raincoat and shook her head. "I made the bumps myself." Papa looked at her face, then slid the blue pot under his arm and opened the bag for hers.

qa.q: How much room did Papa's cloth bag have?
qa.a: It had room for only one pot.

qa.q: Why did Noor call her lumpy pot "the best one"?
qa.a: She shaped it herself ("I made the bumps myself"), so her own effort makes it feel more precious to her than the shiny shop pot.

qa.q: Which choice did Papa Thomas make, and why did it work?
qa.a: He carried the blue pot under his arm and put Noor's pot in the bag, respecting how much her own work meant to her instead of arguing in the rain.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa Thomas in that moment?
qa.a: He is juggling rain, a leaving bus and one small bag, and he had even bought a nicer pot. Still, he can see from Noor's face that the pot she made matters more to her.

grounding: A five-year-old insists her own lumpy clay pot is the best, valuing what she shaped herself over a bought one.

passage: Maria carried her clay pot home from school in both hands, like a bird's egg. It leaned to one side, and her thumbprint was baked right into the rim. In the Panaji flat, Simran Aunty had just come back from the market with a smooth painted pot for the balcony. "Look, Maria, now you have two!" Maria looked at the painted pot, then at hers. She put hers on the dining table, right in the middle. "This one is the best," she said. "I made the thumb." At bedtime, she moved it to the shelf beside her pillow.

qa.q: What was baked into the rim of Maria's pot?
qa.a: Her thumbprint.

qa.q: What does Maria moving her pot beside her pillow suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She treasures it more than the painted pot: she sets it in the middle of the table, calls it "the best" and keeps it close at bedtime, because she made it herself. 🙂

qa.q: How could Simran Aunty respond so Maria feels her work is valued?
qa.a: She could ask Maria to show how she made the thumbprint and help her choose a special spot for her pot, praising the effort rather than comparing which pot is nicer.

qa.q: What might Simran Aunty think when Maria picks the leaning pot?
qa.a: She might be a little surprised, since she brought home a smooth painted pot, but she could also see how proud Maria is of something she made with her own hands.

grounding: A young child treasures the leaning clay pot she made herself over a smooth bought one and calls hers the best.

passage:
"Amma, look! My pot!"
"Karthik, it's leaning like the tower in your picture book."
"It's supposed to lean."
Sabina laughed and held up the glazed pot she'd bought at the Saturday market. "Which one should hold the money plant?"
"Mine."
"The market one has no cracks, kanna."
"Mine has my fingers. See?" He pressed his thumb into the dent.
"Hmm. Shall we put the plant in the market pot, and yours on the windowsill where everyone can see it?"
"No! Mine gets the plant. It's the best pot in the whole house."
Sabina paused, then handed him the little plant. "Okay, gardener. Careful."

qa.q: What did Sabina want one of the pots to hold?
qa.a: The money plant.

qa.q: What does Karthik mean by "Mine has my fingers"?
qa.a: He feels proud of the pot because his own hands shaped it, and that effort makes the cracked, leaning pot the best one to him.

qa.q: Which choice did Sabina make at the end, and what does it show?
qa.a: She handed Karthik the plant for his own pot, choosing to honour his pride in what he made over which pot looked neater. 😊

qa.q: What would change if Sabina had insisted on the market pot?
qa.a: Karthik might feel his work was being called worse, and a proud moment could have turned into tears or a fight.

grounding: A small boy insists his cracked, leaning clay pot is the best in the house because he shaped it with his own fingers.

passage:
Teacher's note, Vasudha, KG-B, Friday:
This week each child shaped a small clay diya pot. Pooja's leans to one side and has a thumb-dent in the rim. Today her mother brought a shiny painted pot from the market for our Diwali corner. Pooja put hers right next to it and said, 'Mine is the best.' When a friend said the painted one was prettier, Pooja held hers against her chest. 'I made the dent.' I let her place hers in front. Next week I'll ask each child what they like about their own pot.

qa.q: What did Pooja's mother bring for the Diwali corner?
qa.a: She brought a shiny painted pot from the market.

qa.q: Why did Pooja hold her pot against her chest?
qa.a: She loved it because she made it herself, and felt it was being unfairly compared with the market pot.

qa.q: What did Vasudha choose to do, and why is it a kind choice?
qa.a: Vasudha let Pooja place her pot in front and plans to ask each child what they like about their own pot, honouring their effort.

qa.q: How might Pooja's friend see the two pots?
qa.a: The friend sees the painted pot as prettier and may not understand why Pooja cares so much about a dent.

grounding: A kindergarten teacher notes a girl who insists her own lopsided clay pot is better than a shiny market one because she made it.

passage: At the weekly haat in their village, Zeenat Apa bought a small red painted pot for her little sister. Dilnaz, five, looked at it and said nothing. That morning, by the pond, she had squeezed her own pot from wet clay. It was flat on one side and had a crack. Back home, Apa put the red pot by the doll's bed. Dilnaz moved it away and put hers there instead. 'This one gives the doll water.' 'It leaks,' Apa said. Dilnaz patted it gently. 'Mine is better. I made it.'

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz make her own pot?
qa.a: She squeezed her own pot from wet clay by the pond.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz say nothing when she first saw the red pot?
qa.a: She already loved the pot she had made herself, so the new red one didn't seem special to her.

qa.q: What could Zeenat Apa do so both pots are valued?
qa.a: She could let Dilnaz keep her pot by the doll's bed and find another spot for the red pot, instead of pointing out the leak.

qa.q: How might Zeenat Apa feel when Dilnaz moves the red pot away?
qa.a: Apa might feel a little hurt that her gift was put aside, and also amused by how much Dilnaz loves her own pot.

grounding: A five-year-old in a village prefers the cracked clay pot she shaped herself over a painted one from the market because she made it.
